title: CJP protest: How to tell reel-makers from journalists? Delhi Police asks SC

ai.summary: Delhi Police clarified that no law requires women protesters to be handled by women officers, and distinguished journalists from social media influencers who create reels during protests.

facts.claim: no mandate requires that women protesters be handled by women officers only
facts.quote: The Delhi Police told the Supreme Court that no mandate requires that women protesters be handled by women officers only
the police argued that the influencers cannot claim the same protections guaranteed to the press while covering protests

facts.claim: reel-makers and social media influencers are not journalists
facts.quote: It remains undetermined whether individuals who make reels and upload them while exploiting the content they create can be elevated to the status of journalists or reporters
At no point was there any deliberate or concerted action on the part of the Delhi Police to obstruct, restrict or interfere with journalists who were lawfully discharging their professional duties
Police said any individual apprehended mistakenly was "immediately released upon verification and ascertainment of their actual identity"

facts.claim: many falsely claimed to be journalists
facts.quote: It reiterated that there were several people in the "illegal protests" who were not journalists "but were using a camera and a microphone, falsely claiming to be journalists"

ai.background_note: Delhi Police clarified distinctions between journalists and social media influencers during protests, addressing allegations of excessive force against reporters at anti-Chief Election Commissioner protests.
